Collaborative Strength Inclusive Growth.

Collaborative Strength Inclusive Growth.
Over four decades ago at Shriram Finance Limited, we established our foundations where traditional banking fell short. We chose the semi-urban corridors and rural markets, extending credit to first-generation entrepreneurs based on real potential rather than rigid paperwork.
Collaborative Strength
Inclusive Growth
The capital and capability from this partnership directly reinforce our primary mission. By introducing global governance standards and advanced technology to India’s under-banked segments, we provide daily-wage workers and rural enterprises with the secure momentum necessary to achieve genuine economic mobility.
MUFG Bank Ltd, a member of MUFG, a global financial group based out of Japan, invested 20% stake in our business. Beyond the immense scale of this cross-border transaction, the alliance creates a distinct structural advantage. It integrates global institutional sophistication with our crystalline grassroots network, combining international financial expertise with the deep-rooted local trust we have spent decades building.
The framework of India’s financial services sector is evolving. By anchoring global scale within our local infrastructure, we harness collaborative strength to accelerate inclusive growth across the nation.

The Story of Mr. Saif,
Chembur Branch, 15 Years
Mr. Saif repaid with discipline and expanded steadily. What started as a single used vehicle became a logistics business operating five heavy trucks. His financial profile grew, and with it, his access to capital from multiple sources.

Mr. Saif repaid with discipline and expanded steadily. What started as a single used vehicle became a logistics business operating five heavy trucks. His financial profile grew, and with it, his access to capital from multiple sources.
Trust is not built in a single conversation. It is built in their accumulation, in the years when things go well and in the years when they do not, in the moments when a lender shows up not just as a financier but as someone who actually knows you.
Mr. Saif's story with Shriram Finance's Chembur branch spans fifteen years of exactly that kind of trust.
Yet today, despite having options, Mr. Saif continues to stay with us. The relationship, he says, extends past lending. It is built on years of trust, understanding and partnership through every stage of his growth.
One Vehicle.
A Beginning
His story reaffirms a conviction that has not changed in four decades: financial inclusion begins with trust, and trust, once earned, has a loyalty that no competing interest rate can easily undo.
with One
Beginning.
the Odds against It

the Odds against It
Our first association was the financing of a pre-owned commercial vehicle, a modest start, but one we made with full commitment. We ensured the process was transparent, respectful and supportive at every step, because we believe that every customer deserves dignity when accessing finance, regardless of where they are starting from.
When Mr. Saif first walked through our door, he was a godown labourer with one specific aspiration: To build a livelihood in the commercial vehicle segment. The challenge was equally specific. Limited documentation. Unstable living conditions. Shared rented accommodation. A profile that most institutions would have turned away at first glance without a second look.
It is a reminder that sometimes, one opportunity backed by genuine belief in a person can create a lifetime of progress.
We looked past the paperwork and at the person. We saw intent, discipline and a work ethic that deserved a chance.

PARTNERING WITH EMPLOYEES
Partnering with Employees The People Who Built the Business
These two journeys, in their beginnings, reflect the same conviction: that Shriram Finance has always been built by people who believe what the institution believes.
The Story of Mr. G.M. Jilani, Joint Managing Director & Chief Operating Officer, Joined as Management Trainee, 1992

The Story of Mr. G.M. Jilani, Joint Managing Director & Chief Operating Officer, Joined as Management Trainee, 1992
The Story of Mr. V. Muruganandapandian, Deputy Managing Director, Joined as Trainee, 1990
A Culture of Decentralised Ownership
Micro-Loans, Massive Impact
What captivated him most was how Shriram ran its branches. A branch manager here carried the autonomy and accountability of a localised CEO. Decisions were made by people closest to the customer, not sent down from the centre. That grassroots-up philosophy runs directly through how Mr. Jilani manages operations today. No major strategy is designed in an ivory tower. It is built on real-time inputs from frontline teams who understand the customer’s reality better than any dashboard can capture.
He pioneered micro-loans as small as Rs. 10,000, structured with a manageable daily repayment of Rs. 100, for grassroots collectives whose work was real but whose paperwork was non-existent. These included the Pookattuvor Sangam: flower garland makers whose income arrived in small, daily amounts; and the Poojarigal Sangam: temple priests who served their communities faithfully but held no salary slips.
Some careers are about climbing. Mr. V. Muruganandapandian's was about going deeper, into the Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns of Tamil Nadu where the idea of formal credit was, for most borrowers, still theoretical.

Some careers are about climbing. Mr. V. Muruganandapandian's was about going deeper, into the Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns of Tamil Nadu where the idea of formal credit was, for most borrowers, still theoretical.
Mr. G.M. Jilani is an architect of scale. He is also, equally, someone who has never lost sight of the individual customer at the centre of every number he manages.
These were hardworking individuals who lacked the documents traditional lending required. They did not lack the character to repay.
When he stepped into Shriram Chits as a management trainee in Andhra Pradesh back in 1992, he found an organisation that matched his own sensibilities. He quickly saw that financial instruments at Shriram were never abstract corporate transactions. They were interwoven with human milestones: a daughter’s wedding, a child’s college admission, the first commercial vehicle a man would call his own.
He started as a trainee in 1990. What he found was not just a job. He found a philosophy: that no dream is too small to fund, if the person carrying it has the intent and integrity to see it through.
Composure as a Leadership Tool

Composure as a Leadership Tool
A Rs. 2 Lakhs loan extended years ago nurtured an aspiring entrepreneur into the proud proprietor of the 3-star hotel chain in Tiruvannamalai. Similar trust fuelled the rise of powerloom operators in Tiruppur and established jewellers across the state. Thousands of truckers who came to Shriram with nothing but a drive to succeed now command multi-crore turnovers.
More than three decades of difficult moments have sharpened rather than softened his resolve. His approach in a crisis has never changed: gather complete data, set the ego outside the room, consult the team and calm a frantic environment through composure rather than volume. He has found consistently, that the leader who stays steady in the chaos is the one the team rallies around.
Leading the Way He Was Taught
Today, Mr. Muruganandapandian leads a business unit of 10,000 colleagues. He credits his team for every milestone and ensures accountability and recognition always travel together, because the culture he built his career in is one of shared success, and he has no intention of changing that now.
The Legacy He Is Building

The Legacy He Is Building
Seeing the young professionals he once mentored now leading pivotal roles across Shriram Finance brings him greater satisfaction than any title. His counsel for those entering the field remains consistent: master your sector with absolute rigour, value long-term growth over a flashy starting package and never stop learning. The moment you stop is the precise moment you start falling behind.
His advice for those entering the organisation is both simple and demanding: Know Your Customer. Prioritise their welfare over pure business metrics. Communicate constantly, because trust is earned in conversation. And spend real time in sales, because that is exactly where lasting relationships are built.

CHAIRMAN’S MESSAGE
Chairman’s Message Collaborative Strength Inclusive Growth
The Realisation of Collaborative Strength
Our frontline teams work closely with communities every day in semi-urban neighbourhoods where emerging entrepreneurs need lenders who recognise their potential, in rural markets where a tractor loan can transform a farming family’s future, and in urban centres where daily-wage earners and small business enterprises gain access to formal credit for the first time. Over the years, this enduring local presence has helped us build a retail credit franchise serving 97.3 Lakhs active customers.

This financial year also marked a defining milestone in our journey, where decades of grassroots credibility converged with global institutional partnership.
In a significant alignment of institutional legacies, our decades of domestic execution came together with the rich global banking heritage of MUFG Bank, spanning nearly one hundred and forty-seven years. The preferential allotment of 47.11 crores equity shares of the Company at Rs. 840.93 per share to MUFG Bank was completed on April 08, 2026.
A borrower base of this scale is more than a business milestone; it reflects the power of inclusive growth. It demonstrates how access to finance at the grassroots level can steadily evolve into a resilient and trusted network, capable of supporting communities through changing economic conditions. This strong on-ground momentum also positioned us to actively participate in India’s broader economic growth during the financial year.
This strategic cross-border investment, valued at approximately Rs. 39,618 Crores (USD 4.4 Billion), resulted in MUFG Bank acquiring a 20% stake in the Company on a fully diluted basis, making it one of the largest strategic transactions in India’s financial services sector.

Advancing the Future of Shared Prosperity
The strategic capital and long-term partnership now position us strongly for the next phase of inclusive growth. We will continue expanding both our physical and digital reach across rural and semi-urban India, ensuring that access to finance remains a meaningful catalyst for livelihoods, mobility, and entrepreneurship.
Financial Proof of Resilient Expansion

Financial Proof of Resilient Expansion
The combination of a strong domestic economy and our time-tested relationship model translated into another year of disciplined and resilient growth. Driven by healthy credit demand across geographies, total Assets Under Management (AUM) crossed the landmark milestone of Rs. 3 Lakh Crores, reaching Rs. 302,274 Crores during the year.
At the same time, we are steadily scaling our commitment to future-ready mobility solutions. Our green financing portfolio is growing towards a targeted AUM of over Rs. 5,000 Crores, supporting electric commercial vehicles, two-wheelers, and clean energy adoption beyond metropolitan centres, while contributing to India’s transition towards a lower-carbon economy.
Profitability remained strong, with Profit After Tax rising to Rs. 9,998 Crores and Net Interest Income increasing to Rs. 26,051 Crores. These results reflect our ability to grow responsibly while maintaining pricing discipline and operational efficiency. Asset quality also remained stable, with Gross Stage 3 assets at 4.58% and Net Stage 3 assets at 2.33%. In recognition of this balance sheet strength, our long-term debt instruments received an upgraded AAA/Stable rating from major credit rating agencies.

Although the near-term global environment continues to require caution amid geopolitical and inflationary pressures, our approach remains firmly anchored in prudence, diversification, and balance sheet resilience. With the support of an expanded Board, the dedication of our frontline teams, and the strength of our global partnership, we step into the next chapter with confidence and optimism.
Dear Stakeholders,
The true identity of Shriram Finance lies in its deep grassroots engagement, over four decades, across India’s underserved credit landscape. From the very beginning, the institution was built on a simple belief: traditional lending systems often overlook hardworking individuals and small enterprises when formal documentation does not fit standard institutional expectations and processes. With this understanding, we shaped a relationship-led lending model and built a network of 3,225 branches where entrepreneurial aspirations first take shape.

At the same time, we accelerated our digital transformation journey by strengthening our credit architecture with AI-enabled identity verification and Account Aggregator data integration. These initiatives led to a considerable reduction in underwriting turnaround time (TAT), improvement in agreement execution TAT and reduction in loan disbursment TAT, ensuring that technology continues to enhance, rather than replace, our signature human touch.
Our commitment remains unchanged to support individual enterprises, strengthen families and communities, and contribute meaningfully to India’s entrepreneurial growth story.

Inclusive growth is realised at the ground level through each carefully assessed credit decision. It is enabled by branch teams that understand their markets deeply, technology platforms that process information with speed and precision and a risk function shaped by decades of experience in complex lending, capable of assessing creditworthiness even in the absence of formal income documentation.

The financial position Shriram Finance enters FY 2026-27 reflects both pillars of our annual theme. Profit After Tax grew 20.87% YoY to Rs. 9,998 Crores in FY 2025-26, alongside a Net Interest Margin of 8.38% and a cost-to-income ratio improved to 27.95%. These are the results of collaborative strength: a large organisation running its financial operations with discipline and genuine coherence across every function. The equity infusion from MUFG Bank has strengthened our capital adequacy considerably, and liquidity coverage remains solid. That capital is what makes inclusive growth scalable. It gives us the financial capacity to extend credit to more customers, in more markets, on the terms our customers need, without compromising the balance between growth, margins and asset quality that this operating environment demands. Optimising borrowing costs and improving productivity remain our immediate priorities, because the efficiency we build today is the capacity for inclusive growth we deploy tomorrow.

Building a lending franchise at the scale Shriram Finance operates requires a specific kind of collaboration: with customers who place their trust in you before the numbers have caught up to their ambition, with markets that others will not enter until the economics have been proven, and with capital partners who understand that the returns compound across years. This collaborative approach, applied for more than four decades, produced a franchise that crossed Rs. 302,274 Crores in AUM in FY 2025-26, growing 14.85% YoY across mobility, MSME and rural segments. The MUFG Bank investment of Rs. 39,618 Crores for a 20% stake, one of the largest cross-border investments India’s financial services sector has seen, is that same collaborative philosophy expressed at its largest scale yet. Two institutions joining their complementary strengths to serve a single direction: inclusive growth across Indian markets that formal finance has not yet fully reached. That is the next chapter, and it is the most ambitious one we have undertaken.

GLOBAL ECONOMIC OVERVIEW
Beyond major power rivalries, instability across several emerging markets is compounding pressures on global trade, investment, and capital flows. Sanctions are changing trade dynamics, increased defence expenditure is redefining priorities, and shifting global alliances are reshaping engagements. In this environment, businesses are promptly evaluating their sourcing models, investment strategies, and long-term geographic exposure. However, the pace of expansion is likely to remain below long-term trends, reflecting the continued impact of trade policy changes, tariff-related developments and geopolitical factors on global trade and investment flows. Shriram Finance Limited (‘Shriram Finance’, ‘The Company’ or ‘We’) is among India’s leading retail-focussed non-banking financial companies, with a presence built across semi-urban and underpenetrated markets where access to formal credit remains uneven. Over time, the Company has shaped a diversified lending platform spanning commercial vehicles, two-wheelers, passenger vehicles, construction and farm equipment, MSME financing, gold loans, personal loans and working capital solutions, reflecting the breadth of credit demand across the Indian economy.
To boost the sector’s growth, the Government has focused on improving formalisation, credit access, and market integration through initiatives such as credit guarantee schemes, digital lending, and Udyam registration. Additional support via export promotion, cluster development, and production-linked incentives is helping MSMEs scale and integrate into value chains. Alongside this, increasing adoption of technology, digital tools, and skill development is enhancing productivity and innovation, positioning MSMEs as key drivers of inclusive and sustainable economic growth.

This has already translated into tangible industry growth, with equipment sales rising sharply in FY 2023–24, led by earthmoving machinery and road construction equipment. Te Mobile Medical Unit (MMU) Program aimed to provide comprehensive primary healthcare support to truck drivers, their families, and underserved communities. Trough mobile medical units stationed at key transport hubs, beneﬁciaries received access to free consultations, diagnostic services, and essential medicines delivered directly to their locations. Each unit is equipped with trained healthcare professionals and supported by digital health systems that enable eﬃcient, personalised care and continuity of treatment. Additionally, the program includes regular health screening camps and awareness sessions on preventive healthcare, hygiene, nutrition, and substance use, empowering beneﬁciaries to adopt healthier lifestyles. By integrating curative, preventive, and promotive healthcare services, the program ensures improved access, early detection of diseases, and overall well-being of the target population.

A contingent liability is a possible obligation that arises from past events whose existence will be conﬁrmed by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events beyond the control of the Company or a present obligation that is not recognised because it is not probable that an outﬂow of resources will be required to settle the obligation. A contingent liability also arises in extremely rare cases where there is a liability that cannot be recognised because it cannot be measured reliably. Te Company does not recognise a contingent liability but discloses its existence in the ﬁnancial statements. Contingent liabilities are reviewed at each balance sheet date.

Non-current assets and disposable groups are classiﬁed as held for sale if their carrying amount is intended to be recovered principally through a sale (rather than through continuing use) when the asset (or disposal Company) is available for immediate sale in its present condition subject only to terms that are usual and customary for sale of such asset (or disposal group) and the sale is highly probable and is expected to qualify for recognition as a completed sale within one year from the date of classiﬁcation except in some circumstances this period can be extended if it is beyond the control of management and there are suﬃcient evidence that the entity remains committed to its plan to sell the asset. Derivatives designated as hedging instruments

(Rs. in crores)
Te Company designates its derivatives as hedging instruments to hedge the variability in cash ﬂows associated with highly probable forecast transactions arising from changes in foreign exchange rates and interest rates. At inception of designated hedging relationships, the Company documents the risk management objective and strategy for undertaking the hedge. Te Company also documents the economic relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument, including whether the changes in cash ﬂows of the hedged item and hedging instrument are expected to oﬀset each other. Tere is an economic relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument as the terms of the cross currency swap contract match that of the foreign currency borrowing (notional amount, interest payment dates, principal repayment date etc.). Te Company has established a hedge ratio of 1:1 for the hedging relationships as the underlying risk of the hedging instruments is identical to the hedged risk components. To test the hedge eﬀectiveness, the Company uses the hypothetical derivative method and compares the changes in the fair value of the hedging instruments against the changes in fair value of the hedged items attributable to the hedged risks.

When a derivative is designated as a cash ﬂow hedging instrument, the eﬀective portion of changes in the fair value of the derivative is recognised in OCI and accumulated in other equity under ‘eﬀective portion of cash ﬂow hedges’. Te eﬀective portion of changes in the fair value of the derivative that is recognised in OCI is limited to the cumulative change in fair value of the hedged item, determined on a present value basis, from inception of the hedge. Any ineﬀective portion of changes in the fair value of the derivative is recognised in the statement of proﬁt and loss.

Gratuity
Te Company has a deﬁned beneﬁt gratuity plan (funded). Te gratuity plan is governed by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. Under the Act, employee who has completed ﬁve years of service is entitled to speciﬁc beneﬁt. Te level of beneﬁts provided depends on the employee’s length of service and last drawn salary. Te fund is managed by third party fund managers.

Te Board of Directors of the Company in its meeting held on April 26, 2024 had approved acquisition of 100% equity stake in Shriram Overseas Investments Private Limited [(now, renamed as Shriram Overseas Investments Limited (‘Shriram Overseas’), w.e.f. June 04, 2025)], subject to approval of RBI. Te RBI has conveyed its approval for the said acquisition vide its letter dated April 01, 2025, subject to compliance with conditions speciﬁed therein. Post compliance of the conditions as speciﬁed in RBI’s approval letter, the Company has acquired 100% equity stake for a purchase consideration of Rs. 50.12 crores in Shriram Overseas. Consequent to acquisition, Shriram Overseas became a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Company w.e.f. May 09, 2025.

Each year, the Board of Trustees reviews the level of funding in the gratuity plan. Such a review includes the asset- liability matching strategy and investment risk management policy. Tis includes employing the use of annuities and longevity swaps to manage the risks. Te Board of Trustees decides contribution to be made by the Company based on the results of this annual review. Te trust is in process of investing entire funds in government securities through third party fund managers and as on March 31, 2026, 94.35 % funds are invested in government securities and balance 5.65% funds are invested in money market and corporate debt instruments. Te Board of Trustees aim to keep annual contributions of the Company relatively stable at a level such that no plan deﬁcits (based on valuation performed) will arise.

Te Company hedges interest rate risks of foreign currency borrowings through derivative transactions. Impairment loss allowance of loans and advances (“Impairment loss allowance”) is a Key Audit Matter as the Company has signiﬁcant credit risk exposure considering the large loan portfolio across a wide geographical range. Te value of loans and advances on the balance sheet is signiﬁcant and there is a high degree of complexity and judgment involved in estimating individual and collective credit impairment provisions, write-oﬀs against these loans and to additionally determine the asset quality and provision of the Company. Te Company’s model to calculate Expected Credit Loss (“ECL”) is inherently complex and judgment is applied in determining the correct construction of the three-stage impairment model (“ECL Model”) including the selection and input of forward-looking information. ECL provision calculation require the use of large volumes of data. Te completeness and reliability of data can signiﬁcantly impact accuracy of the modelled impairment provisions. Te accuracy of data ﬂows and the implementation of related controls are critical for the integrity of the estimated impairment provisions.

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
6. A Company’s internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of ﬁnancial reporting and the preparation of Consolidated Financial Statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A Company’s internal ﬁnancial controls with reference to Consolidated Financial Statements include those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reﬂect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the Company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of Consolidated Financial Statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the Company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the Company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the Company’s assets that could have a material eﬀect on the Consolidated Financial Statements.

Impact of New Labour Codes
A. Shriram Finance Limited (“the Company”):
a) Deﬁned contribution plan

a) Deﬁned contribution plan
Te Government of India has consolidated 29 existing labour legislations into a uniﬁed framework comprising four Labour Codes viz. Code on wages 2019, Codes on Social Security 2020, Industrial Relation Code 2020, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Condition Code 2020 (collectively referred to as the New Labour Codes). Tese Codes have been made eﬀective from November 21, 2025. Te corresponding draf rules under these codes have been issued by the Government.
A deﬁned contribution plan is a pension plan under which the Company pays ﬁxed contributions; there is no legal or
constructive obligation to pay further contributions. Te assets of the plan are held separately from those of the Company in a fund under the control of trustees.
Te Company makes Provident Fund and Employee State Insurance Scheme contributions which are deﬁned contribution
plans for qualifying employees. Under the schemes, the Company is required to contribute a speciﬁed percentage of the payroll costs to fund the beneﬁts. Te Company recognised Rs. 160.01 crores (March 31, 2025: Rs. 168.20 crores) for Provident Fund contributions and Rs. 29.86 crores (March 31, 2025: Rs. 29.12 crores) for Employee State Insurance Scheme contributions in the statement of proﬁt and loss. Te contributions payable to these plans by the Company are at rates speciﬁed in the rules of the schemes.

Employee beneﬁts expenses for the year ended March 31, 2026 include incremental impact on gratuity of Rs. 131.73 crores and on long-term compensated absences of Rs. 65.26 crores due to change in deﬁnition of wages under the New Labour Codes. Te Group continues to monitor the ﬁnalisation of Central/State Rules and clariﬁcations from the Government on other aspects of the New Labour Codes and would provide appropriate accounting eﬀect on the basis of such developments as required.

4. Investment risk: For funded plans that rely on insurers for managing the assets, the value of assets certiﬁed by the insurer may not be the fair value of instruments backing the liability. In such cases, the present value of the assets is independent of the future discount rate. Tis can result in wide ﬂuctuations in the net liability or the funded status if there are signiﬁcant changes in the discount rate during the inter-valuation period.
5. Legislative risk: Legislative risk is the risk of increase in the plan liabilities or reduction in the plan assets due to change in the legislation/regulation. Te government may amend the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, thus requiring the companies to pay higher beneﬁts to the employees. Tis will directly aﬀect the present value of the deﬁned beneﬁt obligation and the same will have to be recognized immediately in the year when any such amendment is eﬀective.

52.02.02: Fair value of the SARs granted Te fair value of the SARs is determined using the Black-Scholes Merton option pricing model. Te fair value and inputs used for determining the fair value of each tranche are given below: Grant I
b. Volatility Volatility is a measure of the amount by which a price has ﬂuctuated or is expected to ﬂuctuate during a period. Te measure of volatility used in the Black-Scholes option pricing model is the annualised standard deviation of the continuously compounded rates of return on the stock over a period of time.

Te period to be considered for volatility must be adequate to represent a consistent trend in the price movements. Accordingly, the annualised volatility has been computed based on the share price data of past one year, from the date of the valuation.
Te fair value is very sensitive to this variable. Higher the volatility, higher is the fair value. Te rationale being, the more volatile a stock is, the more is its potential to go up (or come down), and the more is the probability to gain from the movement in the price. Accordingly, an option to buy a highly volatile stock is more valuable than the one to buy a less volatile stock, since the probability of gaining is lesser in the latter case.

on spreading its lending portfolio across all the states with a cap on maximum limit of exposure for a state and also for an individual/ Group.

57.04.02: Foreign currency risk

57.04.02: Foreign currency risk
Foreign Currency risk is the risk that the value of a ﬁnancial instrument will ﬂuctuate due to changes in foreign exchange rates. Te Group is exposed to foreign currency ﬂuctuation risk for its foreign currency borrowing. Te Group’s borrowings in foreign currency are governed by RBI Master Direction External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations dated March 26, 2019 (as and when updated) which requires entities raising External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) for an average maturity of less than 5 years to hedge minimum 70% of the ECB exposure. Te Group hedges its entire ECB and external commercial bond exposure as per Board approved hedging policy and resource mobilisation policy. Te Group manages foreign currency risk by entering into cross currency swaps and forward contract. When a derivative is entered into for the purpose of being a hedge, the Group negotiates the terms of those derivatives to match with the terms of the hedge exposure. Te Group holds derivative ﬁnancial instruments such as Cross currency interest rate swap to mitigate risk of changes in exchange rate in foreign currency and ﬂoating interest rate. Te Counterparty for these contracts is generally a bank. Tese derivative ﬁnancial instruments are valued based on quoted prices for similar assets and liabilities in active markets or inputs that are directly or indirectly observable in market place. If changes in circumstances aﬀect the terms of the hedged item such that the critical terms no longer match exactly with the critical terms of the hedging instrument, the Group uses the hypothetical derivative method to assess eﬀectiveness.

Since then, he has held various strategic roles within the ﬁrm, primarily in the corporate banking and planning divisions in Japan and in the United States, where he was able to garner extensive relevant experience. Let us first look at the broad economic indicators that have a direct impact or indirect impact on

highlighted the resilience of country's economy, with the data pointing towards strong
consumption, rising investment, and sustained government capital expenditure as the key drivers
of the expansion. The stronger-than-expected performance has reinforced expectation of broad-
based economic momentum across multiple sectors.
The IMF has raised India's GDP growth forecast to 7% for '26-'27, up from 6.4% in July. The
revision in the estimate comes on the back of stronger-than-expected momentum, supported by
resilient domestic demand and robust services activity. India's headline retail inflation rose to
5.4% -- 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August, adding pressure on the country's central
bank to further tighten monetary policy. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in
the world's fastest-growing economy, and has touched 22 months high in September. This
increase is mainly due to higher fuel and food prices, which rose amid West Asia war-driven
supply disruption and delay in seasonal rains. India's food inflation climbed to 7.74% in

chunks.section: Oct 2026 earnings call · Q2 FY2027 · Investor Relations.

supply disruption and delay in seasonal rains. India's food inflation climbed to 7.74% in
September from 5.97% month prior, with prices rising faster than -- faster in rural areas than
cities.
India's wholesale price-based inflation climbed to 11.39% in September from 9.92% in August.
Among key drivers of wholesale inflation were mineral oils, food articles, crude petroleum and
natural gas, coal and lignite, basic metal, chemicals, textile, rubber, plastic product, and electric
equipments. Now, coming to the RBI policy, key takeaway of RBI policy: repo rate increased
by 25 basis point to 5.5 basis point; policy stance shifted from neutral to calibrated tightening;
GDP forecast revised upward to 7.1 from for FY26-'27; CPI inflation forecast '26-'27 raised
marginally to 5.2.
Coming to the rural economy, which has a major impact on our business, the 2023 southwest
monsoon concluded at 87% of long period average, with sharper shortfalls hitting regions like

consumption ahead of crucial festive season, with companies seeing pressure on demand for

faces risk of high oil prices and geopolitical tension.

especially the ongoing crisis in West Asia. India's wholesale price-based inflation also
accelerated over three years high, reaching 3.88% in March from 2.13% in February.

About Shriram Finance Limited.
Shriram Finance Limited is the flagship company of the Shriram group which has significant presence
in Consumer Finance, Life Insurance, General Insurance, Housing Finance, Stock Broking and
Distribution businesses. Shriram Finance Limited is one of India’s largest retail asset financing Non-
Banking Finance Companies (NBFC) with Assets under Management (AUM) above Rs. 3.29 trillion.
Established in 1979, Shriram Finance is a holistic finance provider catering to the needs of Small Road
Transport Operators and small business owners and is a leader in organised financing of pre-owned
commercial vehicles and two wheelers. It has vertically integrated business model and offers financing
number of products which include passenger commercial vehicles, loans to micro and small and
medium enterprises (MSMEs), tractors & farm equipment, gold, personal loans and working capital

Founded in 2011, SAMIL established India's first professionally managed auction platform for pre-owned cars, commercial vehicles, construction equipment, farm equipment, three-wheelers, two-wheelers, and more.

About Us
About Shriram Finance Ltd. Shriram Finance Limited is the flagship company of the Shriram group which has significant presence in Consumer Finance, Life Insurance, General Insurance, Housing Finance, Stock Broking and Distribution businesses. Shriram Finance Limited is one of India’s largest retail asset financing Non-Banking Finance Company (NBFC) with Assets under Management (AUM) above Rs 3.29 trillion. Recently Shriram City Union Finance Limited and Shriram Capital Limited merged with Shriram Transport Finance Company Limited and was subsequently renamed as Shriram Finance Limited. Established in 1979, Shriram Finance is holistic finance provider catering to the needs of Small Road Transport Operators and small business owners and is a leader in organised financing of pre-owned commercial vehicles and two wheelers. It has vertically integrated business model and offers financing number of products which include passenger commercial vehicles, loans to micro and small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), tractors, gold, personal loans and working capital loans etc. Over last 47 years, it has developed strong competencies in the areas of Loan origination, valuation of pre-owned commercial vehicles and other assets, and collections. It has a pan india presence with network of 3,225 branches and an employee strength of 82,292 servicing over 10.57 million customers.

Friday 24th July, 2026, Mumbai : The Board Meeting of Shriram Finance Limited (SFL) was held today
to consider the unaudited financial results for the first quarter ended 30th June, 2026.
Financials (Standalone) :
First quarter ended 30th June, 2026 :
The Net Interest Income for the first quarter ended 30th June, 2026 increased by 33.67 % and stood
at Rs. 8,055.70 crores as against Rs. 6,026.43 crores in the same period of the previous year. The profit

at Rs. 8,055.70 crores as against Rs. 6,026.43 crores in the same period of the previous year. The profit
after tax increased by 59.79 % and stood at Rs. 3,444.56 crores as against Rs. 2,155.73 crores recorded
in the same period of the previous year. The earning per share (basic) increased by 29.41 % and was
Rs. 14.83 as against Rs. 11.46 recorded in the same period of the previous year.
Assets under Management :
Total Assets under Management as on 30th June, 2026 increased by 15.26 % and stood at Rs.
313,798.39 crores as compared to Rs. 272,249.01 crores as on 30th June, 2025 and Rs. 302,273.75
crores as on 31st March, 2026.
About Shriram Finance Limited.
Shriram Finance Limited is the flagship company of the Shriram group which has significant presence
in Consumer Finance, Life Insurance, General Insurance, Stock Broking and Distribution businesses.
Shriram Finance Limited is one of India’s largest retail asset financing Non-Banking Finance
Companies (NBFC) with Assets under Management (AUM) above Rs. 3.13 trillion. Established in 1979,
Shriram Finance is a holistic finance provider catering to the needs of Small Road Transport Operators
and small business owners and is a leader in organised financing of pre-owned commercial vehicles
and two wheelers. It has vertically integrated business model and offers financing number of products

and two wheelers. It has vertically integrated business model and offers financing number of products
which include passenger commercial vehicles, loans to micro and small and medium enterprises
(MSMEs), tractors & farm equipment, gold, personal loans and working capital loans etc. Over last
47 years, it has developed strong competencies in the areas of loan origination, valuation of pre-
owned commercial vehicles and other assets, and collections. It has a pan India presence with
network of 3,225 branches and an employee strength of 78,902 servicing to 103.01 lakhs of customers.

Business Overview
Shriram Automall India Limited (SAMIL), an ISO 9001:2015 & Great Place To Work certified company, is
India’s Largest Phygital Marketplace for Pre-owned Vehicles, Equipment, and other Assets. Founded in 2011, SAMIL pioneered India’s first professionally managed auction platform for pre-owned cars, commercial vehicles, construction equipment, farm equipment, two-wheelers, three-wheelers, and more.
Backed by CarTrade Tech Limited and Shriram Finance Limited, SAMIL operates through a robust pan-
India network of over 131 Automalls and a team of 1600+ professionals. The company conducts thousands of auctions every month through Physical Automalls, Phygital platforms via the MySAMIL App, and digital channels including cartradeexchange.com and bids.samil.in. Through gold.samil.in, SAMIL also facilitates secure and transparent gold auctions for banks and financial institutions.
Beyond auctions, SAMIL offers end-to-end services across the pre-owned asset lifecycle. Adroit Auto
delivers inspection, valuation, and claim settlement services; ThePriceX provides data-driven pricing intelligence; and Augeo enables auctions of properties, plant & machinery, commodities, scrap, salvage, and surplus assets.
